rationale: No panel dissent is carried in the packet. The judgment changed on the ledger, so a complete assessment is returned. What moved it: (1) Bielewicz, Wandelt & Banday 2013 enters the ledger (CCC-E037, E056–E061): a fifth independent reanalysis placing both Gurzadyan–Penrose exemplar directions inside the ΛCDM range over 0–90°, and — more importantly — a positive conventional mechanism (the known anomalous ℓ ≤ 7 multipoles) for the large-radius variance deficit and for the clustering of ring centres, which the incumbent synthesis said no record supplied apart from CCC-E012. The header now says five reanalyses, and the sensitivity analysis on E012 is revised. (2) Jow & Scott 2020 now carries records beyond the marginalization: a third of the Hawking-point excess comes from one point (E054), no anomalous clustering of the top thirty points (E049–E050), no polarization structure (E052–E053), noise ruled out as a confound (E028) — the last of which converts the proponents' WMAP–Planck co-location argument into an expectation under every hypothesis. (3) The erebon thread acquires its first quantitative record: Allen 2020 (E042, E069, E072) puts the gravitational-wave yield of the decay mechanism Penrose described 35–95 orders of magnitude below LIGO, and Nielsen et al. 2019 (E067) removes the correlated-noise premise Penrose adopted; CCC-C505 is graded contradicted and CCC-C007's treatment is rewritten — the case can no longer say 'nobody has looked' as if a search were the missing step. (4) The featured set expands from eleven to nineteen to map the controversy: the proponents' two surviving arguments (CCC-C503 sky-twist, CCC-C504 centre concentration) are featured with honest low/unresolved grades rather than left in the catalog; the low-ℓ competing account (CCC-C523, C524) is featured beside the few-pixel account; the erebon–LIGO conjecture (C505) and Allen's number (C519) are featured; the Warsaw ring claim (C501) and the Hawking-point clustering null (C509) are featured as rungs. Fine-grained children (C502, C508, C510, C511, C512, C525) stay catalogued under their parents and are spanned from the article. (5) The incumbent carried no steelman; one is supplied. loadBearing adds CCC-C503 (the one proponent argument that could reopen the circles branch); weakestLinks adds CCC-C505. Case verdict remains 'contradicted' for the detection claims, with CCC as a cosmology untested rather than refuted. The crux order leads with the preregistered reanalysis, then its prerequisite (quantitative predictions), then the two never-run discriminating tests (fair ellipse null, low-ℓ-conditioned centre test). The article is rewritten to set the four accounts side by side, to carry the Bielewicz, Jow & Scott and Allen material, and to make each 'what would change our mind' visible; the plate stays in the circles section.
accounts: The circles and hot spots are imprints of supermassive black-hole encounters and evaporations in the aeon before our Big Bang, carried across the conformal crossover (CCC)
The features are the ordinary texture of an inflationary ΛCDM sky, certified as anomalous only by an impoverished null ensemble and by statistics chosen after looking
The large-radius variance deficits and the clustering of ring centres are manifestations of the known, unexplained low-order (ℓ ≤ 7) multipole anomalies of the CMB, which predate CCC
The strongest recent signatures are manufactured by a handful of anomalous few-pixel spots that inflate the local variance baseline under the proponents' own search criterion
article:
In November 2010, Roger Penrose — the mathematical physicist whose singularity theorems helped make the Big Bang respectable science — announced that the Big Bang is visible from the far side. With the Armenian mathematical physicist Vahe Gurzadyan, he reported that the microwave sky — the 13.8-billion-year-old radiation that is cosmology's primary document — contains [families of concentric circles over which the temperature varies anomalously little, at significance running as high as six sigma]{claim=CCC-C002}. On the theory the circles were meant to confirm, each family is a scar: the gravitational shock of supermassive black holes colliding, again and again, in a universe that existed before ours.

The theory is Conformal Cyclic Cosmology, and Penrose had stated it in full outline in 2006, four years before anyone went looking for circles. Its starting point is the strangest fact about our beginning: the Big Bang was, gravitationally, in a state of near-perfect order — absurdly low entropy — which is why the Second Law of thermodynamics has had somewhere to go ever since. Penrose replaces "beginning" with "crossover." In the unimaginably remote future, after the last black holes have evaporated, the universe contains almost nothing but massless radiation. To a photon, which experiences no time, an eternity of empty expansion and an initial singularity are — conformally, which is to say up to a change of scale — the same kind of place. CCC takes the identification literally: [the remote future of one aeon becomes the Big Bang of the next, and the previous aeon's black holes leave their marks on our sky]{claim=CCC-C009}, forever.

What sets CCC apart from every other story about "before the Big Bang" is that it walked onto the record and made claims about data everyone already has. Those claims are this case — and so, it turns out, is the question of what it means for a pattern to be surprising.

## Four accounts of one sky

Nobody disputes what is in the maps. The dispute is what put it there, and four accounts are live.

The first is CCC's: the quiet rings are the wavefronts of black-hole collisions in the previous aeon, and a second family of features — compact hot spots — are the final Hawking evaporations of that aeon's largest black holes, funnelled through the crossover. This account predicts circular (not elliptical) rings, spots of a characteristic size, and a sky distribution that traces the previous aeon's clusters.

The second is the standard one: [the sky is a realization of the inflationary ΛCDM model, a correlated random field that is full of structure, and the reported anomalies are what you get when you measure surprise against an impoverished model of chance and quote the best of many searches as if it were the only one]{claim=CCC-C010}. This account predicts that properly simulated skies contain the same rings and spots at the same abundance — and that significance figures will fall when the act of searching is priced in.

The third is a refinement with its own mechanism: [the deficit of variance in large-radius rings is a manifestation of the well-known anomalous distribution of the CMB's lowest multipoles — its largest-scale patterns, ℓ ≤ 7]{claim=CCC-C523}, and [the clustering of low-variance ring centres into a few large regions of sky points to those large-scale features, not to randomly placed sources]{claim=CCC-C524}. The low-multipole oddities are themselves unexplained; they predate CCC and are recorded in the same maps. This account predicts that the ring anomalies vanish when simulations are forced to share the real sky's large-scale pattern.

The fourth is a diagnosis of the search itself: a handful of freak few-pixel spots in the maps inflate the local variance baseline, and the proponents' criterion then certifies the rings around them as anomalously quiet. It predicts that screening those pixels removes the concentric families at full resolution.

The last three are all conventional; they differ in mechanism and are not exclusive. The case's job is to say what the ledger holds for each and what observation would decide among them.

## The circles, examined

{plate:IMG-CCC-P01}

Take the observation first, interpretation second. [Quiet rings in the microwave sky exist — every group that has searched for them finds them]{claim=CCC-C001}, including the theory's fiercest critics, who reproduced the Gurzadyan–Penrose procedure down to its outputs and said so in print: "We do reproduce the claimed ring structures observed in the WMAP data as presented by Gurzadyan and Penrose, thereby verifying their computational procedures," wrote Ingunn Wehus and Hans Kristian Eriksen in Oslo. The dispute begins one step later, at a question that sounds too simple to fight over: compared to what?

*Significance* means: unlikely under the null hypothesis — the model of what the sky would look like if nothing interesting were happening. Gurzadyan and Penrose computed theirs against simulated skies of pure Gaussian randomness plus instrument noise. Within weeks, three independent groups — Wehus and Eriksen; Adam Moss, Douglas Scott and James Zibin in Vancouver; Amir Hajian, who also modelled WMAP's spatially varying noise realistically — ran the same search against skies simulated from the standard cosmological model, whose fluctuations are correlated across the sky in precisely measured ways. In those richer simulated skies the circles appeared in the same abundance as in the real one. Moss, Scott and Zibin's verdict became the episode's epitaph: Gurzadyan and Penrose "have not found evidence for pre-Big Bang phenomena, but have simply re-discovered that the CMB contains structure."

Remarkably, the proponents agreed about the fact while contesting the moral. ["Both groups simulate maps using the CMB power spectrum for LCDM, while we simulate a pure Gaussian sky plus the WMAP's noise," they wrote — and insisted that a sky simulated with the standard model's spectrum smuggles the very structure in question into the definition of chance]{claim=CCC-C003}. Their reply added that the circles occur in *concentric families*, which "cannot be explained as a purely random effect" — an assertion the ledger records as made, not quantified.

Two further reanalyses closed the remaining exits. In 2013 Paweł Bielewicz, Benjamin Wandelt and Anthony Banday scanned ring radii from 0° to 90° around the two Gurzadyan–Penrose exemplar directions and found no significant number of unusually extreme variances against ΛCDM simulations; any other point in the same region near the north ecliptic pole, they noted, "shows a similar number of unusually low variance rings." In 2015 Angelo DeAbreu, Dagoberto Contreras and Douglas Scott froze the search to the proponents' own published parameters — a de facto prespecification — extended it to the newer Planck data, confirmed the special directions were there, and found them "at the same level of abundance in simulated Gaussian CMB skies." Five independent groups, five verdicts, one method of disagreement.

### The low-multipole account

Bielewicz and colleagues did more than add a null. They found that the systematically low variance of rings larger than about 10° around the exemplar direction (105°, 37°) [is removed when the ℓ ≤ 7 multipoles of the simulations are replaced by the values the real sky actually has]{claim=CCC-C512} — that is, once the simulated skies share our sky's known large-scale peculiarities, the deficit is no longer unusual. They also observed something the CCC picture does not naturally produce: the deficit is systematic across all large radii from that centre, whereas a series of discrete collision shells should yield some low rings among ordinary ones. Their conclusion is blunt — "our results are not consistent with the conformal cyclic cosmology scenario" — but it turns on a reading of CCC (randomly distributed ring centres) that the proponents dispute, a disagreement about what the theory predicts that is itself part of the story below.

### The few-pixel account

The finest-resolution search yet, by Eve Bodnia and colleagues in 2024, found a trapdoor under the whole method: "spots consisting of a few unusually bright (high-temperature) or dark (low-temperature) pixels, erroneously lead to regions with many low-variance circles, and consequently sets of near-concentric low-variance circles, when applying the search criteria used in previous work. After removing those spots from the data, no statistically significant low-variance circles can be found." The code is open-source. The diagnosis explains false concentric families around anomalous spots; it does not by itself account for every family reported earlier, and the authors say so.

### What the proponents still hold

Fairness requires the other side of the ledger. The proponents' strongest reply is the "sky-twist" test, published in 2013 in a refereed venue: if the concentric families are relics of expanding spherical wavefronts they should be circular, and [Gurzadyan and Penrose report that the prevalence of concentric sets drops dramatically when the search looks for even slightly elliptical rings — a comparison of the sky against distorted versions of itself, with no simulations to argue over — and that ring radii reach about 15° but never exceed 20°]{claim=CCC-C503}. A second Warsaw-based statistic reported [ring-type structures in WMAP at 99.7% confidence against artificial maps of the same harmonic content]{claim=CCC-C501}, and [a Planck follow-up at 99.4%]{claim=CCC-C502}. And the proponents point to the sky distribution: [the centres of concentric ring triples are extravagantly clumped — about 83% of 1134 centres lying within three regions covering roughly 3% of the searched sky]{claim=CCC-C504} — which they read as superclusters in the previous aeon.

Here the ledger is honest about its gaps. No independent group has re-run the sky-twist test with an appropriate null: the statistic and its expected behaviour under chance were introduced in the paper that reported its success, and the one published objection to it is known to the ledger only through the proponents' rebuttal, which calls it "a point which is actually irrelevant to the analysis." The Warsaw figures rest on a statistic chosen after looking, by authors who later co-signed the Hawking-points paper. The clumping of centres is real — Bielewicz and colleagues independently found low-variance rings clustering in a few large regions — but the two camps predict opposite things from CCC about it (random centres versus supercluster imprints), and the low-multipole account offers a conventional cause that has never been tested against the specific 83%-in-3% statistic. These are the live items of the circles branch, and they are desk work.

## The Hawking points

By 2018 the proponents had moved to a second signature. A supermassive black hole from the previous aeon does not only collide; eventually it evaporates, and CCC says its entire Hawking-radiation output arrives through the crossover as a compact hot spot. Daniel An, Krzysztof Meissner, Paweł Nurowski and Penrose reported exactly that: [a population of raised-temperature spots with angular radii of 0.03–0.04 radians and a clear cut-off at that size, present in the Planck maps at 99.98% confidence against 10,000 simulations]{claim=CCC-C004}, with the five strongest spots sitting at the same sky locations in the WMAP data — two instruments, different noise, one signal. They added that clustering of these spots "could be further evidence of CCC."

The independent examination, by Dylan Jow and Douglas Scott, is a small manual of statistical hygiene, and it makes four separate cuts.

First, the *look-elsewhere effect*: the 99.98% was quoted for the ring size that worked best, after the size was chosen by looking. Marginalize — average fairly — over the family of sizes actually searched, and "an excess is detected in Planck satellite maps at only an 87% confidence level (i.e., little more than 1σ)." One sigma is weather.

Second, fragility: about a third of the excess at the claimed scales comes from the single most significant point, and [dropping the two most significant points raises the probability of getting such a result by chance above 10%]{claim=CCC-C511}. A population signal should not live in two features.

Third, clustering: [the thirty most significant points show no anomalous clustering — their mean nearest-neighbour separation, 0.20 and 0.19 radians at the two claimed scales, sits within one sigma of the Gaussian-sky expectation of 0.20 ± 0.03]{claim=CCC-C509}. The proponents' proposed "further evidence" is absent.

Fourth, the other channel: [stacking Planck's E-mode polarization maps on the temperature-selected spots shows no corresponding structure]{claim=CCC-C510} — though, as Jow and Scott themselves note, CCC makes no polarization prediction, so this null constrains nothing in the theory as stated. It is a target for any future prediction, not a refutation.

Two more searches followed. Marcos López and colleagues built a ring detector, validated it on synthetic Hawking points constructed according to CCC — recovering 95% of them — and applied it to four Planck maps: "no significant ring-like structures were observed," with a small candidate excess at the 1% level honestly reported. Bodnia and colleagues' machine-learning search, HawkingNet, likewise finds nothing significant and can rule out spots between 100 and 400 microkelvin with Gaussian widths of 0.7–1.2 degrees outright.

What of the WMAP–Planck coincidence, which no critic has specifically dismantled? Jow and Scott's noise test speaks to it indirectly: adding Planck half-difference maps as a noise estimate does not alter the probability distributions, so instrumental noise is negligible at these scales. If the strongest features are features of the sky at all — as any real hot spot in a ΛCDM sky is — both instruments must see them in the same place. Co-location proves the spots are in the sky rather than in the electronics. It does not say which universe they came from.

The proponents have not answered these cuts in the same terms. A 2025 preprint by Meissner and Penrose instead elaborates the signal: a "gravitational wave epoch" around the crossover, a mass–energy conservation law across it, and a relation tying each spot's temperature rise to the mass of its source cluster in the previous aeon, reported to agree with the largest clusters we observe. It also explains why the spots are about twice the angular size that should have been expected — by the new epoch. The preprint is unreviewed, its calculation checked by no one outside the program, and it treats as "impressive observational evidence" a detection whose statistical existence the marginalization dissolved. A signal's detailed properties cannot be evidence while its existence is unrehabilitated. But the mass–temperature relation is the first CCC-derived fragment of a quantitative signal model, and that matters below.

## Erebons: the prediction that touched a detector

CCC's most concrete forward commitment is about dark matter. Because the theory deletes inflation, [the burden of explaining the almost scale-free texture of the CMB falls on the previous aeon's dark matter, decaying during that aeon's exponential expansion]{claim=CCC-C008}. And the theory says what that dark matter is: [Planck-mass particles Penrose names erebons — about 10⁻⁵ grams, interacting only gravitationally, born at the crossover, decaying with a lifetime of "perhaps something like" 10¹¹ years — whose decays in our own aeon might register in gravitational-wave detectors]{claim=CCC-C007}.

In 2017 Penrose took that last clause to the data. A Copenhagen group had reported that the residual noise in LIGO's two detectors around the first detected event, GW150914, is cross-correlated with a maximum at the same time lag as the event itself. [Penrose proposed that this apparent noise might be gravitational impulses from erebon decays in the host galaxy of the black-hole merger — the merger "serving merely to locate an individual galaxy in the sky" — and specified a test: look for correlated noise at the time delay corresponding to a prominent galaxy such as Andromeda, without waiting for a merger at all]{claim=CCC-C505}.

No one has run that test. But the ledger now holds two records that bear on whether running it could find anything. Alex Nielsen and LIGO-affiliated colleagues report that after subtracting a maximum-likelihood waveform rather than the illustrative template the Copenhagen group used, "there are no statistically significant correlations between the residuals" of the two detectors at GW150914 — on this analysis the premise Penrose adopted is a template artifact, not a property of the noise. (The case records this paper's finding while noting its text has not yet been fully verified for the ledger.) A 2026 preprint extending the cross-correlation test to nine later events and all three detector pairs finds the event-window peaks statistically indistinguishable from off-source noise in 26 of 27 measurements, without mentioning CCC; it keeps the question open at most.

More decisive is a calculation Bruce Allen published in 2020, "originally motivated by Penrose's conformal cyclic cosmology." For Planck-mass dark-matter particles with lifetimes longer than the age of the universe decaying to gravitons, [the direct gravitational-wave background at LIGO frequencies is below 2 × 10⁻¹⁰³ in the standard energy-density units — about 95 orders of magnitude under LIGO's limit]{claim=CCC-C519}; even the larger "memory-effect" contribution "misses detectability by 35 orders of magnitude." Allen's model is a homogeneous cosmological population, not a nearby impulsive event, and Penrose stresses galactic concentrations a hundred times denser — but a factor of a hundred does not bridge thirty-five powers of ten. The result constrains the detectability of erebon decay under the emission Penrose described; it says nothing about whether erebons are dark matter, and Allen notes it applies to any neutral scalar particle decaying to two massless ones. What it does mean is that the erebon–detector prediction is not waiting for a search. It is waiting for an emission mechanism that could produce a signal — or a proof that none can.

## The theory's own bill

The construction's costs are itemized by its author and its friends. For the far future to forget its scale, every particle with rest mass must eventually shed it — [a "mass fade-out" that Penrose calls "an admittedly unconventional hypothesis," for which no accepted particle-physics mechanism exists]{claim=CCC-C005}; the electron, whose decay charge conservation forbids, is the sharpest case, and Paul Tod — the relativist who built CCC's crossover equations — lists "Can one implement mass fade-out?" among the theory's open questions, alongside whether the familiar spectrum of density perturbations can be derived from the previous aeon. Penrose's mitigation is that with a positive cosmological constant, mass is not an invariant of the relevant symmetry group and so need not be fixed.

The entropy bookkeeping is stranger still. [Each aeon can start clean only if black holes genuinely destroy information, and the conformal rescaling at crossover resets the gravitational entropy]{claim=CCC-C006} — a position most of quantum gravity rejects. Michał Eckstein's 2023 analysis argues that "the assumed loss of degrees of freedom in black holes is not compatible with the quantum notion of entropy" and that information loss as Penrose describes it raises global entropy rather than resetting it — while proposing a unitary variant that preserves CCC's observational program. The mechanism rung is therefore not a wash: one published attack, one sympathetic inventory of open problems, no independent derivation of the reset.

Against all this stands the rival's scorecard. The Planck 2018 inflation analysis fits the ΛCDM-plus-inflation framework to temperature, polarization and lensing data with a measured red tilt, tight Gaussianity limits and parameter-level agreement of simple slow-roll models. CCC must reproduce that before its distinctive signatures add net evidence. The one inflationary signature still unseen is the primordial gravitational-wave background in the CMB's B-mode polarization: BICEP/Keck and partners bound the tensor-to-scalar ratio to r < 0.036. Many viable inflation models sit below that, so the null damages nothing yet — but a confirmed detection would evidence an inflationary era in our own aeon that CCC, having deleted inflation, cannot supply. It is the rare place where the theory is exposed to data it has not already survived.

## Where the dispute actually lives

Step back and the pattern is unusually clean. There is no dispute about the sky: every feature the proponents report, the critics reproduce. There is no dispute about the mathematics of the theory: the crossover equations are worked out and their open problems catalogued by sympathetic hands. The entire evidentiary contest has collapsed into methodology — which ensemble defines "expected," how to price the act of searching, and what a-posteriori pattern-finding is worth.

[Across the twelve searches on the record from 2010 to 2024, on both sides, the operative signal model — statistic, size window, thresholds, expected abundance — was supplied by the searchers, never derived from CCC; and no reported significance, positive or negative, was produced under a protocol fixed before the data were examined]{claim=CCC-C011}. Hajian said so in 2011; Bielewicz noted CCC gives no established prediction even for ring width; Bodnia and colleagues made it their synthesis; Jow and Scott observe that their conclusion could only have been avoided if "the predictions of CCC could have been made much more precise" before looking. The proponents chose their statistics after exploring the maps; the critics chose theirs after reading the proponents; each new proponent argument arrived after the previous one was answered, and the proponents' own view of the critiques is that they "are not demonstrations that such signals do not actually exist, but indicate that a more sophisticated analysis is needed." The Bielewicz-versus-proponent disagreement over whether CCC predicts random or clustered ring centres is the same deficit seen from inside: a theory whose signal model is under-specified can be read as predicting either.

This is not a symmetric sin. A null result obtained under the claimant's own frozen criteria — DeAbreu and colleagues did exactly that — carries a weight a post-hoc positive does not, and a positive significance that dissolves whenever a free choice is varied is not the same kind of finding as five nulls that agree. But the asymmetry explains why the same sky keeps signing affidavits for both parties, and it caps the critical case too: nobody preregistered anything.

## What would change our mind

The searches are desk work on public data with open-source tooling. What has never existed is a protocol both camps endorsed before unblinding — statistic, ensemble, mask, artifact screen, look-elsewhere correction, all frozen, then applied once to the final Planck maps. Either outcome is decisive for the existing claims. Three narrower tests would decide among the accounts in this article:

- **A fair ellipse null for the sky-twist test.** Compute from simulations how annular variance should behave for ellipses of increasing eccentricity, then run the concentric-set search on real and simulated skies. If the real sky prefers circles and the simulated skies do not, the circles branch reopens and the proponents' best argument is vindicated; if the eccentricity dependence tracks the simulations, it falls.
- **The centre concentration against low-multipole-conditioned skies.** Reproduce the 83%-in-3% statistic on standard ΛCDM skies and on skies forced to share our ℓ ≤ 7 pattern. If conditioned skies routinely reach such concentrations, the low-multipole account wins; if neither ensemble approaches it, the clumping becomes the strongest surviving proponent observation.
- **Quantitative predictions.** How many circles, how bright, how shaped; how many spots, at what amplitude, with what polarization and sky distribution. The 2025 mass–temperature relation is one fragment. Until the model exists, positive claims cannot be credited and nulls cannot be fatal — the definition of a dispute that can run forever.

On the framework: a primordial B-mode detection would count against CCC, and proponents could sharpen the test by stating in advance what value of r the theory cannot survive. On the erebons: a decay mechanism that produces a computable strain at a detector — or a demonstration that no gravitationally coupled Planck-mass decay can — would turn the LIGO conjecture back into a search or retire it. And on the theory: a field-theoretic mass fade-out consistent with the electron's stability, or a no-go theorem, would restructure the case regardless of the sky.

The universe before this one is not a foolish idea. It is a serious idea whose observational case has so far failed review — brought by a great physicist, examined by competent critics, and stuck at an impasse that is methodological rather than cosmic. The sky is not going anywhere. What the case is waiting for is a protocol, and a theory precise enough to be bound by one.

assessment.synthesis: The ladder has a credible bottom rung that decides nothing and a broken second rung. The annular low-variance features and the ring-like hot spots are genuine outputs of the published procedures, reproduced on WMAP and Planck by hostile groups (CCC-E002, CCC-E008, CCC-E037); a feature both ΛCDM and CCC skies produce separates nothing. One step up, the anomaly claims fail: five independent reanalyses place the circles at chance abundance — Wehus & Eriksen, Moss/Scott/Zibin, Hajian, Bielewicz et al. and DeAbreu et al., the last freezing the proponents' own parameters (CCC-E002, E003, E004, E037, E008); the Hawking-point 99.98% falls to about 87% under size marginalization (CCC-E010), a third of the residual comes from a single point (CCC-E054), the proposed clustering is absent (CCC-E049, E050), and a detector validated at 95% retrieval on synthetic CCC signals finds no significant population (CCC-E011). The null-ensemble crux both camps state in print (CCC-E005) is argued by proponents but never quantified against the ΛCDM ensemble, and Bielewicz et al. show it is subtler than 'Gaussian versus ΛCDM': even ΛCDM skies must be conditioned on the observed ℓ ≤ 7 multipoles before the large-radius deficit becomes typical (CCC-E056, E057), which supplies a positive conventional mechanism for the two features the proponents still hold — the systematic large-radius deficit and the clustering of centres. The few-pixel diagnosis (CCC-E012) supplies a second positive mechanism, for the concentric families under the proponents' criterion. Attribution (CCC-C009) therefore has nothing left to stand on, and the one recent proponent paper (CCC-E022) elaborates a signal whose statistical existence is unrehabilitated. The erebon route, CCC's laboratory-adjacent prediction, now has its first calculation: Allen 2020 places the gravitational-wave yield of the decay Penrose described 35–95 orders of magnitude below LIGO (CCC-E042, E069), and the correlated-noise premise Penrose adopted is removed on the maximum-likelihood analysis (CCC-E067, on a source not yet fully verified), so CCC-C505 is contradicted and CCC-R002 is downstream of a mechanism (CCC-R008), not merely unrun. Sensitivity: the single record whose removal would most change the case verdict remains CCC-E012, the only record reaching both signatures and supplying a false-positive generator; the verdict survives its removal — E002, E003, E004, E008, E037 sustain 'contradicted' on the circles and E010, E011, E054 on the Hawking points — and, unlike before, confidence on CCC-C002 would stay high, because Bielewicz et al. now supply an independent positive account of the large-radius and clustering features. The verdict attaches to the specific detection claims, not to CCC as a cosmology, which is untested rather than refuted; and because no search on either side was preregistered (CCC-E023), the critical case is capped too. Verdicts on the mechanism rungs (CCC-C005, C006) lean partly on priors about mass conservation and unitarity, and the reasoning says so.
assessment.steelman: The strongest case for CCC's signatures that this assessment does not answer runs as follows. (1) The sky-twist test (CCC-C503) compares the real sky against distorted copies of itself, so it is immune to the null-ensemble objection that dispatched every other proponent statistic; it has never been independently re-run with an appropriate null, and the one objection to it is known to the ledger only via the proponents' rebuttal. (2) The concentration of concentric-triple centres — 83% of 1134 in 3% of sky (CCC-C504) — is a real, independently observed clustering; the low-multipole mechanism offered for it (CCC-C524) was established on a different statistic in 2013 and has never been tested against this figure. (3) The five strongest Hawking-point candidates co-locate in Planck and WMAP, and the marginalized residue is 87%, with López et al. reporting a 1%-level candidate excess: the nulls leave non-zero residues rather than zeros. (4) Every null was computed against a signal model the searchers invented; CCC could be right and every search mis-aimed, as Bodnia et al. themselves concede in stating their nulls 'do not disprove the CCC model'. (5) The theory predates the searches by four years (CCC-E014), and the 2025 Meissner–Penrose mass–temperature relation reportedly matches the largest observed clusters — the first derived prediction to make contact with the data. (6) Allen's erebon bound assumes a homogeneous population and a spherically symmetric impulsive decay; a non-spherical decay or a nearby galactic source is not computed. None of this changes a verdict: (1), (2) and (4) are exactly the items the research agenda prioritizes because they are open, not because they are won; (3) is expected under every hypothesis once noise is shown negligible (CCC-E028); (5) elaborates a signal whose existence is unrehabilitated; (6) is a task (CCC-R008), not a result.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: The universe cycles through aeons. As each aeon's matter decays toward masslessness, its exponentially expanded remote future becomes conformally identical to the next aeon's Big Bang, so information can cross the boundary. Supermassive black-hole encounters late in the previous aeon emitted gravitational radiation that registers in our cosmic microwave background as families of concentric low-variance circles; the final Hawking evaporation of such black holes deposits compact spots of raised temperature ('Hawking points'). Proponents claim both are present in WMAP and Planck data — circles at up to 6σ, ring-type structures at 99.7% and 99.4%, Hawking points at 99.98% confidence — that the circles are circular rather than elliptical and their centres clumped, that dark matter consists of decaying Planck-mass 'erebons' created at the crossover, and that erebon decays may already appear as correlated noise in gravitational-wave detectors.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether the sky contains the features — every group that has looked, critical groups included, reproduces the low-variance circles and the hot spots, and the clustering of ring centres is independently observed. The crux is the null hypothesis and the accounting for the search. Gurzadyan and Penrose computed significance against a pure Gaussian sky plus instrument noise; five independent reanalyses, simulating skies with the full ΛCDM power spectrum, find the same features at the same abundance in synthetic data containing no previous aeon, and one shows the large-radius deficit becomes typical once simulations share the real sky's anomalous ℓ ≤ 7 multipoles. Layered on top: a-posteriori statistics (the Hawking-point confidence falls from 99.98% to about 1σ when the ring size is not chosen after looking, and a third of the residue comes from one point), and a 2024 diagnosis that few-pixel bright spots manufacture concentric low-variance circles under the proponents' criteria. Two proponent arguments remain untested rather than refuted: the sky-twist circularity preference and the 83%-in-3% centre concentration; the two camps also disagree about what CCC predicts for the distribution of centres. On the forward prediction, the disagreement is whether any erebon decay could produce a detectable signal at all: the only calculation says no by tens of orders of magnitude under the emission Penrose described.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: A preregistered, adversarial reanalysis — statistic (including the sky-twist ellipticity test), simulation ensemble, mask, few-pixel artifact screen and look-elsewhere correction fixed jointly by proponents and critics before unblinding — applied once to the final Planck maps would settle the existing detection claims. Two narrower desk tests would decide among the accounts: a fair ellipse null for the sky-twist statistic (does the real sky prefer circles when simulated skies do not?) and a re-run of the concentric-triple centre statistic on ΛCDM skies conditioned on the observed ℓ ≤ 7 multipoles (do conditioned skies reach 80% concentration?). Quantitative CCC predictions — abundance, amplitude, profile, polarization, sky distribution — would make every search interpretable; the 2025 mass–temperature relation is one fragment. Independently: a confirmed detection of primordial tensor B-modes would establish an inflationary signal CCC has no mechanism for; a specified erebon-decay emission mechanism that survives Allen's isotropy result would reopen a detector search, or a proof that none can would close it; and a field-theoretic mass fade-out or a no-go theorem would restructure the theory rung regardless of the sky.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Standard inflationary ΛCDM, plus the ordinary statistics of searching. The CMB is a realization of a correlated Gaussian random field with a red-tilted power spectrum; such a field is full of structure, including rings of low variance and compact warm spots, at exactly the abundance the reanalyses find. The proponents' significance figures arise from comparing the sky to an impoverished null (a Gaussian sky without the observed correlations), from selecting statistics and search parameters after inspecting the data, and — for the strongest recent claims — from a handful of anomalous few-pixel spots that inflate the local baseline variance and thereby generate concentric low-variance circles around themselves. The systematic large-radius deficits and the clustering of ring centres into a few large regions are manifestations of the known, still unexplained anomalies of the CMB's lowest multipoles, which predate CCC and require no previous aeon. The WMAP–Planck co-location of the strongest spots is expected under every hypothesis once instrumental noise is shown negligible at those scales. On this account nothing pre-cosmic has been detected; the CMB has been re-discovered to contain structure.

components.label: The concentric-circles claim
components.note: Features real and reproduced; anomaly dissolved by five independent reanalyses using ΛCDM ensembles; two positive conventional mechanisms (low-ℓ multipoles, few-pixel spots); the sky-twist and centre-concentration arguments remain untested rather than refuted.

components.label: The Hawking-points claim
components.note: 99.98% falls to ~87% under size marginalization; a third of the residue from one point; no anomalous clustering; two independent detectors validated on synthetic CCC signals find no significant population; cross-map co-location is expected under any hypothesis.

components.label: The null-hypothesis dispute
components.note: Both camps agree in print that the disagreement is the ensemble; no search on either side was preregistered; the signal model has been supplied by searchers in all twelve searches on the record.

components.label: The conformal bridge (theory rung)
components.note: Mass fade-out required and admittedly unconventional with no mechanism; entropy reset attacked by Eckstein 2023 and listed open by Tod 2022; the 2025 crossover conservation law is unreviewed progress.

components.label: Erebons and forward predictions
components.note: A genuine forward commitment, but the LIGO-noise conjecture's premise is removed on the maximum-likelihood analysis and the only calculation puts the yield 35–95 orders of magnitude below detectability; the perturbation spectrum is not derived.

components.label: The inflationary ΛCDM steelman
components.note: Precision-fit framework; its one undetected signature (tensor B-modes, r < 0.036) is the open discriminator that could count against CCC.

researchPriority.reason: The detection claims are already contradicted by five independent reanalyses and two independent Hawking-point searches, so no live anomaly demands urgent resources. What remains is cheap and decisive desk work — a preregistered joint protocol, a fair ellipse null for the sky-twist test, and a low-ℓ-conditioned test of the centre concentration — that would close or reopen the case at negligible cost; the theory items (quantitative predictions, mass fade-out, an erebon emission mechanism) are open-ended and carry the higher leverage per page if anyone in the program takes them up.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The attribution depends on CCC-C002 and CCC-C004, both contradicted: five independent reanalyses place the circles at chance abundance (CCC-E002, E003, E004, E008, E037), the Hawking-point significance dissolves under marginalization and is dominated by two points (CCC-E010, E054), and independent detectors validated on synthetic CCC signals find nothing (CCC-E011, E012). Bielewicz et al. add that the systematic large-radius deficit and regional clustering are inconsistent with discrete collision shells as they read CCC (CCC-E058–E060). The 2025 preprint (CCC-E022) defends the interpretation without rehabilitating the detection. Priority of the theory (CCC-E014) is recorded and does not bear on whether the specific signatures are present.

treatment.plainLanguage: The quiet rings and hot spots in the microwave sky are scars left by black holes in a universe before ours.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis; if the features were shown anomalous and circular, it would be the only account on the table that predicted them in advance.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every independent group reproduces the features and finds them at the same abundance in skies simulated without a previous aeon; the only proponent arguments not so tested (sky-twist, centre concentration) have never been independently run.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered joint reanalysis (CCC-R001) in which a circle or spot excess survives artifact screening and look-elsewhere correction.
A fair ellipse null (CCC-R006) showing the real sky prefers circles when simulated skies do not.
Low-ℓ-conditioned ΛCDM skies (CCC-R007) failing to reproduce the 83%-in-3% centre concentration.
A CCC-derived quantitative signal model (CCC-R005) whose predicted abundance, amplitude and profile match the data where ΛCDM's do not.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Five independent circle reanalyses (CCC-E002, E003, E004, E008, E037), the Hawking-point marginalization (CCC-E010), the few-pixel false-positive generator (CCC-E012) and the low-multipole mechanism (CCC-E056) together account for every reported signature, and the framework itself is the most precisely fitted model in cosmology (CCC-E020). The word 'fully' is the claim's exposure: the sky-twist statistic (CCC-C503) and the specific 83%-in-3% concentration (CCC-C504) have not been re-run under conventional nulls, and BICEP/Keck's null on tensor modes (CCC-E021) leaves the inflationary sector's signature unconfirmed.

treatment.plainLanguage: An ordinary inflationary sky, searched hard enough with statistics chosen after looking, produces everything the proponents report.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The direct rival to CCC-C009; the evidence that supports it is the evidence that contradicts the thesis.
treatment.strongestObjection: It has not been demonstrated for the sky-twist circularity preference or the concentric-triple centre concentration, and a-posteriori statistics were also used by the critics.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A surviving excess in a preregistered protocol (CCC-R001).
A circularity preference in the data absent from ΛCDM simulations (CCC-R006).
A centre concentration unreachable by low-ℓ-conditioned ΛCDM skies (CCC-R007).

claimAssessments.reasoning: Wehus & Eriksen, Moss/Scott/Zibin, Hajian, Bielewicz et al. and DeAbreu et al. (CCC-E002, E003, E004, E037, E008) all reproduce the circles and find them at chance abundance against ΛCDM ensembles, the last with the proponents' own frozen parameters and Planck data; Bodnia et al. (CCC-E012) find no significant circles at full resolution after removing few-pixel spots and identify how they are manufactured; Bielewicz et al. (CCC-E056, E057) supply a positive mechanism for the large-radius deficit. The supporting records (CCC-E001, E006, E007) compute significance against a pure Gaussian null or with statistics introduced post hoc (CCC-E023). Rests on the ensemble question (CCC-C003), which the proponents contest but have never quantified.

treatment.plainLanguage: The concentric quiet rings are too unlikely to be chance in a standard sky.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The founding rung; if it held, the thesis would have an anomaly to explain.
treatment.strongestObjection: The proponents hold that ΛCDM-spectrum simulations import the disputed structure into the definition of chance, and their sky-twist test avoids simulations entirely and has never been independently re-run.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered search (CCC-R001) finding the concentric families at significance after artifact screening.
A quantitative demonstration that concentric families specifically (not single rings) are rare in ΛCDM ensembles.
The fair ellipse null (CCC-R006) confirming a circularity preference.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Jow & Scott reduce the 99.98% to about 87% by marginalizing over the ring size chosen after looking (CCC-E010), show a third of the residual excess comes from one point (CCC-E054), find no anomalous clustering (CCC-E049, E050) and no polarization counterpart (CCC-E052, E053); López et al.'s detector, validated at 95% retrieval on synthetic CCC spots, finds no significant population (CCC-E011); Bodnia et al. rule out spots of 100–400 µK and 0.7–1.2° (CCC-E012). The supporting record (CCC-E009) is proponent-authored with a post-hoc size choice; its cross-map co-location argument is expected for any sky feature once noise is negligible (CCC-E028).

treatment.plainLanguage: The Planck and WMAP maps contain a population of hot spots of a special size that a standard sky would not produce.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The program's strongest published claim; a genuine population of size-cut-off hot spots would be hard for ΛCDM to produce.
treatment.strongestObjection: The five strongest spots sit at the same sky locations in two instruments with different noise, and no critic has specifically dismantled that coincidence; the marginalized residue is 87%, not zero.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered search (CCC-R001) with the spot size fixed in advance by a CCC-derived prediction that finds an excess.
A profile or amplitude prediction (CCC-R005) under which López et al.'s and Bodnia et al.'s detectors would have been insensitive.
A polarization or clustering prediction that the stacks and nearest-neighbour statistics then confirm.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Hostile groups reproduce the ring structures and verify the computational procedures (CCC-E002, E008); Bielewicz et al. find low-variance rings around the exemplar directions and elsewhere (CCC-E037, E058); Moss/Scott/Zibin confirm the variance variations exist (CCC-E003).

treatment.plainLanguage: There really are directions on the sky around which rings of the map are unusually quiet, and anyone running the published search finds them.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Both ΛCDM and CCC skies produce such rings; their existence separates no account.
treatment.strongestObjection: None serious; the only caveat is that the features' existence is sometimes cited as if it were their anomaly.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Failure of an independent group to reproduce the ring structures from the published procedure — no such failure is on record.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Stated in the proponents' own words (CCC-E005) and matched by the critics' descriptions of their ensembles (CCC-E002, E003, E004). Bielewicz et al. refine it: within ΛCDM ensembles, conditioning on the observed ℓ ≤ 7 multipoles is what renders the large-radius deficit typical (CCC-E056, E057), so the crux is the ensemble's large-scale content as well as its spectrum. The proponents' contention that the ΛCDM ensemble is the wrong null is asserted, not quantified.

treatment.plainLanguage: The two sides get different answers because they simulate different versions of a boring sky.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Locates the disagreement precisely; it does not by itself say who is right, but it explains why every proponent significance dissolves under reanalysis.
treatment.strongestObjection: It understates a second source of disagreement — post-hoc choice of statistic — which persists even when ensembles agree, as the Hawking-point episode shows.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A demonstration that concentric families are rare even in ΛCDM ensembles conditioned on the observed low multipoles.
Evidence that the critics' ensembles mis-model the data in a way that produces spurious rings.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The study table (CCC-E023) documents twelve searches from 2010–2024 in which the signal model was supplied by the searchers; the proponents' rejoinder (CCC-E013), Jow & Scott's counterfactual (CCC-E055) and Bielewicz et al.'s note that CCC gives no established ring-width prediction corroborate it; the incompatible proponent and critic readings of what CCC predicts for ring-centre distribution (CCC-E058–E060 versus CCC-C504) illustrate the under-specification.

treatment.plainLanguage: Nobody on either side fixed their method before looking at the sky, so every number reflects choices made after the fact.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Explains the stalemate and caps both sides; it does not itself favour either account, though the asymmetry (nulls under frozen proponent parameters) is recorded.
treatment.strongestObjection: It treats the sin as symmetric when DeAbreu et al.'s frozen-parameter null is a de facto prespecification.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered protocol deposited and executed (CCC-R001).
A CCC-derived signal model published before a search (CCC-R005).

claimAssessments.reasoning: The report is verified (CCC-E006) and appears in a refereed venue, but the statistic and its null behaviour were introduced in the paper reporting its success (CCC-E023), no independent group has run it, the one published objection is known to the ledger only through the proponents' rebuttal (CCC-E013), and Bodnia et al. note few-pixel spots could interact with the ellipticity comparison in unassessed ways (CCC-E012). 'Unresolved' is a finding: this is the one proponent argument that is neither confirmed nor refuted on the record.

treatment.plainLanguage: The proponents say the concentric families only show up when you look for perfect circles, not squashed ones — which is what real spherical shockwaves would do.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If a circularity preference exists in the data and not in simulated skies, the circles branch reopens; if it tracks simulations, the proponents' best argument falls.
treatment.strongestObjection: The sky-rotation procedure used to generate approximate ellipses may change the expected variance profile itself, making the comparison unfair — an objection the ledger records only via the proponents' dismissal of it.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A fair ellipse null (CCC-R006) showing the data's eccentricity dependence tracks ΛCDM simulations — would move to contradicted.
The same test showing a circularity preference absent from simulations — would move to supported and reopen CCC-C002.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The reported concentration figure is in the 2020 paper and the non-isotropy was reported in 2013 (CCC-E006); Bielewicz et al. independently find low-variance rings clustering in a few large regions (CCC-E058, E061), so the clustering itself is observed by two groups. The interpretation is contested: Bielewicz et al. attribute it to large-angular-scale features (CCC-C524), and the two camps read CCC as predicting opposite distributions. The specific 83%-in-3% statistic has not been tested against any conventional ensemble.

treatment.plainLanguage: The centres of the concentric ring sets pile up in three small patches of sky.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Real clustering, but a conventional mechanism exists and CCC's own prediction for centre distribution is disputed between camps; on its own it decides little.
treatment.strongestObjection: Clustering in a few large regions is what the known low-multipole anomalies would produce, and the same clustering was read by an independent group as inconsistent with CCC.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Low-ℓ-conditioned ΛCDM skies (CCC-R007) routinely reaching ~80% concentration — would relocate the clumping to the conventional account.
Neither ensemble approaching it — would make this the strongest surviving proponent observation.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The report is verified in a Royal Society venue (CCC-E007, weak) but the statistic and threshold were chosen post hoc, the group is proponent-adjacent, and the study table records the 99.7% figure among the significances that dissolved under reanalysis (CCC-E023). No independent replication of this statistic is on record.

treatment.plainLanguage: A Warsaw group found ring-shaped patterns in the WMAP map that appear in only 0.3% of artificial maps with the same overall statistics.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A second post-hoc statistic from the same program; it does not escape the ensemble and search-accounting objections that dissolved the founding claim.
treatment.strongestObjection: Comparing against maps 'of the same harmonic content' preserves the power spectrum but not the choice of statistic after inspection.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent group applying the same statistic under a preregistered protocol and recovering the 99.7% excess.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Jow & Scott report mean nearest-neighbour separations of 0.20 and 0.19 rad against a Gaussian-sky expectation of 0.20 ± 0.03 (CCC-E049, E050); the analysis uses only 100 simulations and the top thirty points at two scales, and Planck 2018 rather than the proponents' 2015 data.

treatment.plainLanguage: The strongest hot-spot candidates are spread across the sky exactly as random ones would be.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Removes a proposed 'further evidence' for CCC; a null clustering result is consistent with both accounts.
treatment.strongestObjection: Thin simulation sample and a small point set; a weaker clustering signal could hide below its sensitivity.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A larger simulation ensemble showing the data's separation is anomalous.
A CCC prediction of expected clustering strength that this test would have missed.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Bielewicz et al. show the large-radius deficit around (105°,37°) is removed when the ℓ ≤ 7 multipoles of the simulations are replaced by the data's (CCC-E056, E057; catalogued detail CCC-C512), and attribute the ring anomalies to the known low-order anomalies. One independent group, WMAP7 only, not re-run on Planck; the low-ℓ anomalies are themselves unexplained, so this relocates rather than dissolves the oddity.

treatment.plainLanguage: The big quiet rings are a side-effect of the already-known strangeness of the sky's largest-scale patterns.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A positive conventional mechanism for the one feature ΛCDM nulls left unexplained; if it holds, the large-radius rings need no previous aeon.
treatment.strongestObjection: The low-multipole anomalies are unexplained in ΛCDM too, and the demonstration is on a single WMAP7 direction.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Failure of the conditioning to remove the deficit on Planck 2018 maps or at other exemplar directions.
A CCC-derived prediction that ties the large-radius rings to the low multipoles in a way ΛCDM does not.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Bielewicz et al. state that clustering of low-variance rings in relatively large regions 'rather indicates effects related to large angular scale features' (CCC-E056, E057, E061), and their rotation test supports it; but their statistic (extreme-variance ring counts per centre) differs from the 2020 concentric-triple statistic, and the specific 83%-in-3% figure has not been tested.

treatment.plainLanguage: The ring centres bunch up because the sky's largest patterns bunch them, not because something in a previous universe was clustered.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The conventional rival to the proponents' supercluster reading of CCC-C504; the two make different predictions for low-ℓ-conditioned simulations.
treatment.strongestObjection: It has never been applied to the concentric-triple centre statistic on which the proponents' 83% figure rests.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Low-ℓ-conditioned ΛCDM skies (CCC-R007) failing to reproduce the centre concentration.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Penrose states the requirement and calls the mechanism 'an admittedly unconventional hypothesis' (CCC-E015); Tod lists 'Can one implement mass fade-out?' as open, noting massless charged particles are problematic (CCC-E016); the 2025 preprint derives a crossover conservation law but supplies no fade-out mechanism (CCC-E022). The claim concerns the theory's cost, and the verdict leans on the prior that charge conservation forbids electron decay.

treatment.plainLanguage: For the theory to work, every particle must eventually lose its mass, and nobody knows how that could happen.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A standing theoretical debt; it does not bear on the sky statistics but sets the prior against which the signatures are weighed.
treatment.strongestObjection: With a positive cosmological constant, mass is not a Casimir invariant of the de Sitter group, so asymptotic fade-out is not obviously forbidden.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A field-theoretic implementation consistent with electron stability and charge conservation (CCC-R004).
A no-go theorem, which would move the whole theory rung to contradicted.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Penrose's account exists in his 2013 paper and book; Eckstein argues that information loss as described raises global entropy and undermines the 'entropy renormalisation' (CCC-E017) while offering a unitary repair; Tod treats the conformal-factor choice as open (CCC-E016). One published attack, one sympathetic inventory, no independent derivation of the reset; the verdict leans on priors about unitarity in quantum gravity.

treatment.plainLanguage: The theory's answer to why each new universe starts tidy depends on black holes truly erasing information — which most physicists doubt, and one analysis says would make things messier, not tidier.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Bears on CCC's motivating problem, not on the CMB claims; a unitary variant preserves the observational program either way.
treatment.strongestObjection: Black-hole information loss has defenders, and Eckstein's own repair shows the framework can survive without it.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent derivation showing the crossover rescaling resets gravitational entropy consistently with quantum entropy.
Consensus resolution of the information paradox against loss.

claimAssessments.reasoning: As a description of what CCC predicts, the claim is verbatim from Penrose 2018 (CCC-E018) and 2017 (CCC-E019). Its detector clause is now qualified: Allen 2020 finds the gravitational-wave background from the decay Penrose describes 'far too weak to observe with LIGO or other instruments' (CCC-E072), by 35–95 orders of magnitude (CCC-E042, E069), while explicitly not constraining erebons as dark matter (CCC-E070, E071). The parameters ('perhaps,' 'or thereabouts') remain order-of-magnitude.

treatment.plainLanguage: CCC says dark matter is made of tiny Planck-mass particles born at the crossover that slowly decay — and that their decays might show up in gravitational-wave detectors.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A genuine forward commitment most pre-Big-Bang proposals lack; but the only computed yield says the detector route cannot test it as stated.
treatment.strongestObjection: Under the emission mechanism Penrose describes, the signal is tens of orders of magnitude below any detector, so the prediction is presently untestable rather than testable-and-pending.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A specified non-spherical decay model with a computable single-event strain and rate (CCC-R008).
A derivation of the CMB perturbation spectrum from erebon decay (CCC-R004).
A dark-matter direct-detection or structure result inconsistent with gravitation-only Planck-mass particles.

claimAssessments.reasoning: 'There is no inflation in CCC' is Penrose's own statement (CCC-E018); the erebon-decay origin of the fluctuations is asserted, not derived — Tod lists deriving the spectrum as open (CCC-E016). BICEP/Keck's r < 0.036 (CCC-E021) leaves the inflationary tensor signature undetected, so the discriminator is open in both directions.

treatment.plainLanguage: CCC has no inflation; it says the near-uniform texture of the microwave sky comes from dark-matter decay in the previous universe.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The one place CCC is exposed to data it has not already survived: a confirmed primordial B-mode detection would evidence an inflationary era CCC cannot supply.
treatment.strongestObjection: The perturbation spectrum has not been derived from erebon decay, so CCC currently owes what inflation delivers with precision (CCC-E020).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A confirmed detection of primordial tensor B-modes (CCC-R003) — would count against CCC.
A CCC derivation reproducing the measured tilt and Gaussianity — would discharge the debt.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The proposal and its specified test are verified (CCC-E019, E064). Its premise — correlated LIGO noise maximized at the event's lag (CCC-E062, unverified source) — is not reproduced after maximum-likelihood waveform subtraction (CCC-E067, on a source the ledger has not fully verified); the 2026 preprint is context only (CCC-E077). The decisive verified record is Allen 2020: the memory-effect background from the decay Penrose described misses LIGO by 35 orders of magnitude (CCC-E069), the direct background by 95 (CCC-E042). Allen's model is a homogeneous population; Penrose's galactic concentration argument buys a factor of order 100, not 10³⁵.

treatment.plainLanguage: Penrose suggested the mysterious matching noise in LIGO's two detectors might be dark-matter particles decaying — but the noise seems to be an analysis artifact, and the predicted signal is unimaginably too faint.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even if erebons exist, this route cannot presently detect them, so its failure does not test CCC; its success would have been transformative.
treatment.strongestObjection: Allen computes a stochastic background from an isotropic decay; a nearby, non-spherical impulsive event is not modelled, and the Nielsen analysis relies on a general-relativity waveform to construct residuals.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An emission mechanism (CCC-R008) yielding a computable strain within detector reach.
An erebon-decay search (CCC-R002) at the Andromeda time delay returning coincident transients above a preregistered threshold.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Directly from Allen 2020 §III, Eq. (5), a CC-BY refereed Rapid Communication (CCC-E042); the limit compared is the LIGO O1+O2 bound. Single calculation, narrow model by construction (homogeneous population, two-graviton decay).

treatment.plainLanguage: If Planck-mass dark matter decays straight into gravitons, the resulting hum is about a hundred billion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion times too quiet for LIGO.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Closes the direct-graviton route to detection; it constrains detectability, not whether erebons exist.
treatment.strongestObjection: A different decay channel or geometry could in principle radiate differently — which is exactly what CCC-R008 asks proponents to specify.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent recalculation finding an error of tens of orders of magnitude.
A specified decay channel outside Allen's model class.
